A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same hybrid cognitive-modeling framework and original arithmetic study. Despite the changed title and substantial expansion, their text, equations, figures, tables, Methods, and appendices support reliable matching and comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports an original arithmetic user study, statistical analyses of collected responses, and trained-model evaluations, including response-time prediction and training efficiency.

after.justification: v4 retains those original empirical results and adds model evaluations and ablations on the CPC18 decision-making and PeerEdu learning datasets.

M1.justification: The original four-stage arithmetic framework is retained. Appendix A.11.2 adds an LSTM risk-prediction agent for decision making and a text-embedding agent for learning. The learning adaptation introduces median-based curiosity classification alongside continuous-value prediction and adjusts DRL observations, actions, and rewards, substantially extending the procedure and its outputs.

E1.justification: v3 evaluates arithmetic reasoning under four time-pressure conditions. v4 retains this coverage and adds CPC18 gambling decisions with numeric feedback (30,489 trials, 240 participants) and PeerEdu learning with textual peer feedback and continuous curiosity outcomes (12,804 samples, 300 students), as documented in Section 5 and Appendix A.11.

E2.justification: Beyond v3's Pure DRL and SVM comparisons, v4 evaluates hGRU, LSTM models with pretrained visual encoders, Transformers, MLPs, decision trees, random forests, and linear regression in the arithmetic comparison (Tables 1 and 4). It also introduces DL-plus-DDM comparators, including an MLP architecture matched to the hybrid agent (Figure 11).

E3.justification: The original general, group, individual, and LOPO evaluation designs remain. Added comparisons introduce five task/feedback encoding configurations and validation-based epoch selection: Appendix A.9 divides the original 80% training portion into 80% training and 20% validation, with 30- or 100-epoch budgets for different baseline families. The new learning evaluation also applies MAPE to continuous curiosity.

E4.justification: The original feature-representation, LSTM-width, and Hybrid-versus-Pure-DRL analyses are retained. v4 adds user/trial aggregation analyses of prediction-error variability, component-removal studies on the new tasks, and DL-plus-DDM controls across all three datasets to investigate the contribution of reinforcement learning (Sections 4.1 and 5; Figures 4 and 11).

E5.justification: v4 substantially expands model-comparison statistics with MAPE standard deviations, distribution percentiles, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov and permutation tests (Tables 3–8; Figure 11). Table 4 labels the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range of individual errors as a confidence interval. These additions concern error distributions and significance reporting; neither PDF establishes repeated-training run counts or an increase in runs.

E6.justification: The original general-level Hybrid/Pure DRL MAPEs of 0.2999/0.3034 remain (v3 Figure 6; v4 Figure 2). v4 adds numerous baseline and ablation results, including numeric-input CogReact MAPE 0.2703 and CPC18/PeerEdu MAPEs 0.357/0.950 (Table 4; Figure 4). These concern added encodings or tasks. The explicit attention/anxiety ANOVA findings from v3 are omitted, although their descriptive plots remain.

T1.justification: The evidence-scaling formula, response-time and termination relations, and reward equations (1)–(2) are retained in Appendices A.7–A.8. v4 adds implementation explanations, including naming Brownian noise, but no new formal theoretical development, derivation, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: v3's principal claims concern logical reasoning under time pressure, with broader applicability proposed prospectively. v4's abstract, contribution list, and conclusion claim demonstrated applicability across arithmetic, decision making, and learning, including continuous cognitive states and multiple feedback modalities. This substantially broadens the claimed contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations attributing error variability to user/trial differences and performance benefits to complementary DDM and RL components. It also argues that task embeddings can benefit DRL despite worsening standalone SVM predictions (Section 5). The explicit population-diversity limitation in v3's Discussion disappears, while Appendix A.10 adds possible extensions to neural and physiological evidence trajectories.

D1.justification: v4 newly specifies adaptive-feedback thresholds and the greater-than-three-hour participant exclusion criterion, and supplies extensive baseline architectures, optimization settings, training times, and hardware details. It identifies the text-embedding model used for PeerEdu and replaces the separate OSF/ReactiveAI access statements with a CogReact repository reference. The additional original-study details do not establish that its procedures changed.

R1.justification: v4 substantially updates its research positioning around contemporary cognitive simulation, reaction-time models, and language-model-based cognition, adding works such as Goetschalckx et al. (2024), Binz and Schulz (2024), and PeerEdu. It connects evaluated baselines to these research strands and removes several earlier robotics, interaction, and synthetic-data application references.

P1.justification: The paper is renamed CogReact and extensively reorganized into numbered Related Work, Methodology, Evaluation, Generalization, and Discussion sections. Much of v3's dataset exploration and Methods material moves into detailed appendices, while the abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten.

P2.justification: v4 changes the single-column presentation to a two-column layout, adds baseline/statistical tables, cross-task result plots, and detailed Hybrid/Pure DRL architecture diagrams. Original figures are matched across relocation and renumbering; notably, v3 Figure 4's SVM bar panel becomes v4 Table 3, while the remaining panels become Figure 9.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens comparative validation: relevant additional baselines and DL-plus-DDM controls address alternative explanations left open by v3, while evaluated adaptations to two additional cognitive tasks support previously prospective generalization claims. Expanded implementation details also improve reproducibility. Mislabeling error percentiles as confidence intervals and dropping the explicit population-diversity caveat weaken reporting, but the stronger experimental tests provide a clear, substantial net improvement.
